warmup.q: An FX feed emits a rate every 100 ms. Dashboard A subscribes at 0 ms, dashboard B at 250 ms, both to feed.share(). What does B receive first?
options: The first rate, because share() replays from the start
The rate emitted at 200 ms, because share() keeps the latest
warmup.why: share() is publish().refCount(): one upstream subscription, multicast to whoever is subscribed when an item arrives. B joined at 250 ms, so its first item is the one at 300 ms. Replaying the latest is replay(1).refCount(), and replaying everything is cache().

sections.h: Cold sources run per subscriber; hot ones are shared
sections.html:
A cold publisher does its work again for every subscriber (lesson 2 of this track). That is right for an HTTP call per request. It is wrong for a WebSocket of FX rates that six dashboards open: six connections to the provider, six copies of the same ticks. A hot publisher produces whether or not anyone listens, and subscribers share what it produces from the moment they join.

Reactor turns cold into hot with a few operators. They differ in two decisions: when to connect to the source, and what a subscriber that joins late receives.

Operator Connects A late subscriber gets Disconnects
share(), which is publish().refCount() at the first subscriber only new items when the last one leaves
replay(n).refCount() at the first subscriber the last n items, then new ones when the last one leaves
publish().autoConnect(n) when n have subscribed only new items never
cache() at the first subscriber every item, from the start never

In the demo a feed emits a rate every 100 ms and dashboard B joins at 250 ms. Cold, B opens a second connection and starts from the first rate. With share(), B gets only the rates from 300 ms on. With replay(1).refCount(), B immediately gets the 200 ms rate, then the live ones. With cache(), B gets all of them, including the two it missed, and the cache keeps every item for as long as the Flux lives. For a long-running feed that is a memory leak, so prefer replay(n) or cache(n). Mono.cache(ttl) is the right tool for a value that should be reloaded now and then, such as a fee schedule.

Two details matter in production. publish follows the slowest subscriber: it requests from the source only what every subscriber can take, so one slow dashboard slows them all (combine it with a policy from lesson 7 of this track). And refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)) adds a grace period: when the last subscriber leaves, it waits 5 seconds before disconnecting, so a dashboard that refreshes the page doesn't make you reconnect to the provider.

try.title: Five ways to share one feed
steps: HotColdDemo runs a cold feed (a rate every 100 ms, five rates) with dashboard A subscribing at once and B 250 ms later. It tries cold, share(), replay(1).refCount(), cache() and publish().autoConnect(2).
For each run, predict the number of connections and what B receives.
Run it. Then explain the autoConnect(2) line: why does A get all five rates, starting late?

code.title: HotColdDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** One cold FX feed, shared five ways between dashboard A (starts now) and dashboard B (joins 250 ms later). */ public class HotColdDemo { static final AtomicInteger connections = new AtomicInteger(); // a cold feed: every subscriber opens its own connection and gets rates from the start, one per 100 ms static Flux<String> rateFeed() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(5) .map(i -> "1.08" + i) .doOnSubscribe(s -> connections.incrementAndGet()); } static void run(String title, Flux<String> feed) throws InterruptedException { connections.set(0); List<String> a = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<String> b = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(2); feed.doFinally(signal -> done.countDown()).subscribe(a::add); Thread.sleep(250); feed.doFinally(signal -> done.countDown()).subscribe(b::add); done.await(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-28s connections=%d%n%5sA=%s%n%5sB=%s%n", title, connections.get(), "", a, "", b); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("1. cold", rateFeed()); run("2. share()", rateFeed().share()); run("3. replay(1).refCount()", rateFeed().replay(1).refCount()); run("4. cache()", rateFeed().cache()); run("5. publish().autoConnect(2)", rateFeed().publish().autoConnect(2)); } }

alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val connections = AtomicInteger() // a cold feed: every subscriber opens its own connection and gets rates from the start, one per 100 ms private fun rateFeed(): Flux<String> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(5) .map { i -> "1.08$i" } .doOnSubscribe { connections.incrementAndGet() } private fun run(title: String, feed: Flux<String>) { connections.set(0) val a = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() val b = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() val done = CountDownLatch(2) feed.doFinally { done.countDown() }.subscribe { a += it } Thread.sleep(250) feed.doFinally { done.countDown() }.subscribe { b += it } done.await(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("%-28s connections=%d%n%5sA=%s%n%5sB=%s".format(title, connections.get(), "", a, "", b)) } /** One cold FX feed, shared five ways between dashboard A (starts now) and dashboard B (joins 250 ms later). */ fun main() { run("1. cold", rateFeed()) run("2. share()", rateFeed().share()) run("3. replay(1).refCount()", rateFeed().replay(1).refCount()) run("4. cache()", rateFeed().cache()) run("5. publish().autoConnect(2)", rateFeed().publish().autoConnect(2)) }

try.expect: Cold: 2 connections, and both get all five rates. share(): 1 connection, B gets 1.082 to 1.084. replay(1).refCount(): B also gets 1.081 the moment it subscribes. cache(): B gets all five. autoConnect(2): 1 connection that opens only when B subscribes at 250 ms, so both get all five, and A waited 250 ms for its first rate.

sections.h: Sinks push values in from ordinary code
sections.html:
Sometimes the values come from ordinary code: a Kafka listener callback, a webhook handler, a scheduled job. Sinks is Reactor's safe way to push them into a Flux. (Processors used to do this; Reactor has phased them out in favour of Sinks.)

Java
Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort();
Flux<PaymentEvent> live = sink.asFlux();                    // what subscribers see
Sinks.EmitResult result = sink.tryEmitNext(event);          // what the listener calls
Kotlin
val sink: Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()
val live: Flux<PaymentEvent> = sink.asFlux()                // what subscribers see
val result: Sinks.EmitResult = sink.tryEmitNext(event)      // what the listener calls

Sinks.many().multicast() sends each item to the subscribers present at that moment, in three flavours. onBackpressureBuffer() buffers for slow subscribers and keeps items pushed before the first subscriber arrives for it. By default it also shuts down for good when its last subscriber leaves: a subscriber that comes later just receives onComplete. directBestEffort() keeps no buffer: a subscriber that isn't asking misses the item, and the sink keeps working with zero subscribers. directAllOrNothing() drops the item for everyone if one subscriber isn't ready. Then many().replay() keeps history for late subscribers (all(), limit(n), limit(Duration), latest()), many().unicast() allows exactly one subscriber, and Sinks.one() and Sinks.empty() carry a single value or a bare completion.

The trap is threads. tryEmitNext never blocks and never retries. If two threads call it at the same moment, one of them gets EmitResult.FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its item is not emitted. This is rule 1.3 from lesson 1 of this track at work: a subscriber must never get two signals at once. The sink detects the overlap, and instead of breaking the rule, it fails the second call. Ignore the result and items vanish. In my runs of the demo, 8 threads emitting 10,000 items each delivered only a few thousand of the 80,000.

Either check every result, or call emitNext(item, handler) with a handler that retries. Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) spins until the sink is free, for up to a second. Its Javadoc asks you not to keep and reuse it, so create one per call. Wrapping the emit in a lock works too.

try.title: Who gets what from a sink
steps: SinksDemo pushes values into a multicast sink before and between two subscribers, checks two multicast flavours after every subscriber has left, fills a replay().limit(2) sink, tries two subscribers on a unicast sink, and finally lets 8 threads emit 10,000 items each, first with tryEmitNext, then with emitNext and busyLooping.
Predict each line before you run it. For the race, guess how many of the 80,000 items arrive.
Run it twice and compare the race numbers.

code.title: SinksDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.BiConsumer; /** Sinks push values into Reactor from ordinary code. Who receives what, and what happens with 8 threads? */ public class SinksDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Integer> multicast = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); List<Integer> early = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Integer> late = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); multicast.tryEmitNext(10); // nobody is subscribed yet multicast.asFlux().subscribe(early::add); multicast.tryEmitNext(1); multicast.tryEmitNext(2); multicast.asFlux().subscribe(late::add); multicast.tryEmitNext(3); System.out.println("1. multicast: early=" + early + " late=" + late); afterEveryoneLeft("onBackpressureBuffer()", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer()); afterEveryoneLeft("directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()); Sinks.Many<Integer> replay = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); replay.tryEmitNext(1); replay.tryEmitNext(2); replay.tryEmitNext(3); List<Integer> lateReplay = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); replay.asFlux().subscribe(lateReplay::add); System.out.println("3. replay().limit(2): late=" + lateReplay); Sinks.Many<Integer> unicast = Sinks.many().unicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); unicast.asFlux().subscribe(); unicast.asFlux().subscribe(v -> { }, e -> System.out.println("4. unicast, second subscriber: " + e.getMessage())); race("5. tryEmitNext from 8 threads", (sink, i) -> { if (sink.tryEmitNext(i).isFailure()) failures.incrementAndGet(); }); race("6. emitNext + busyLooping", (sink, i) -> sink.emitNext(i, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))); } static void afterEveryoneLeft(String flavour, Sinks.Many<Integer> sink) { sink.asFlux().subscribe().dispose(); // the only subscriber leaves List<String> next = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(v -> next.add("got " + v), e -> next.add("error"), () -> next.add("completed")); sink.tryEmitNext(42); System.out.printf("2. %-22s after everyone left, a new subscriber %s%n", flavour, next); } static final AtomicInteger failures = new AtomicInteger(); static void race(String title, BiConsumer<Sinks.Many<Integer>, Integer> emit) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Integer> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); AtomicInteger received = new AtomicInteger(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(v -> received.incrementAndGet()); failures.set(0); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < threads.length; t++) { threads[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) emit.accept(sink, i); }); threads[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-32s received %,d of 80,000 (%,d emits failed)%n", title, received.get(), failures.get()); } }

alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val failures = AtomicInteger() private fun afterEveryoneLeft(flavour: String, sink: Sinks.Many<Int>) { sink.asFlux().subscribe().dispose() // the only subscriber leaves val next = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() sink.asFlux().subscribe({ v -> next += "got $v" }, { next += "error" }, { next += "completed" }) sink.tryEmitNext(42) println("2. %-22s after everyone left, a new subscriber %s".format(flavour, next)) } private fun race(title: String, emit: (Sinks.Many<Int>, Int) -> Unit) { val sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() val received = AtomicInteger() sink.asFlux().subscribe { received.incrementAndGet() } failures.set(0) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() repeat(10_000) { i -> emit(sink, i) } } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-32s received %,d of 80,000 (%,d emits failed)".format(title, received.get(), failures.get())) } /** Sinks push values into Reactor from ordinary code. Who receives what, and what happens with 8 threads? */ fun main() { val multicast = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() val early = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() val late = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() multicast.tryEmitNext(10) // nobody is subscribed yet multicast.asFlux().subscribe { early += it } multicast.tryEmitNext(1) multicast.tryEmitNext(2) multicast.asFlux().subscribe { late += it } multicast.tryEmitNext(3) println("1. multicast: early=$early late=$late") afterEveryoneLeft("onBackpressureBuffer()", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer()) afterEveryoneLeft("directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()) val replay = Sinks.many().replay().limit<Int>(2) replay.tryEmitNext(1) replay.tryEmitNext(2) replay.tryEmitNext(3) val lateReplay = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() replay.asFlux().subscribe { lateReplay += it } println("3. replay().limit(2): late=$lateReplay") val unicast = Sinks.many().unicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() unicast.asFlux().subscribe() unicast.asFlux().subscribe({ }, { e -> println("4. unicast, second subscriber: ${e.message}") }) race("5. tryEmitNext from 8 threads") { sink, i -> if (sink.tryEmitNext(i).isFailure) failures.incrementAndGet() } race("6. emitNext + busyLooping") { sink, i -> sink.emitNext(i, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))) } }

try.expect: Multicast: early=[10, 1, 2, 3] (the 10 waited in the warm-up buffer) and late=[3]. After everyone left, the onBackpressureBuffer() sink only completes the new subscriber, while directBestEffort() delivers got 42. Replay with limit 2: [2, 3]. Unicast: the second subscriber fails with Sinks.many().unicast() sinks only allow a single Subscriber. The tryEmitNext race delivers only a few thousand of 80,000, with a different number each run; emitNext with busyLooping delivers all 80,000.

sections.h: StepVerifier checks the signals, and virtual time fakes the clock
sections.html:
A reactive test has to subscribe, check each signal in order, and fail when anything else happens. StepVerifier from reactor-test does that:

Java
StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "c-1"))
        .expectNext(expectedQuote)
        .expectComplete()
        .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
Kotlin
StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "c-1"))
    .expectNext(expectedQuote)
    .expectComplete()
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1))

Four rules, each learned from a test that lied:

  1. Nothing runs until verify() (or a shortcut such as verifyComplete() or verifyError()). A test that ends at expectComplete() never subscribes, and passes whatever the code does.
  2. verify() has no timeout by default, so a hung publisher hangs the build. Pass a Duration, or set StepVerifier.setDefaultTimeout(...) once.
  3. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> ...) replaces Reactor's schedulers with a virtual clock, so a one-day delay is verified in milliseconds. Build the publisher inside the supplier: a Mono.delay built earlier has already picked the real clock, and the test times out.
  4. expectNoEvent(d) checks that nothing happens during d of virtual time. The subscription counts as an event, so put expectSubscription() first.

For a source you drive by hand there is TestPublisher: call next(...), complete() or error(...) from the test, then check wasCancelled() or assertMinRequested(n). TestPublisher.create() respects demand like a real source and fails if pushed without it; createNoncompliant(...) breaks the spec on purpose (lesson 1 of this track). PublisherProbe answers a different question: was this branch subscribed at all? Use it to prove that a switchIfEmpty fallback ran, or didn't. All the virtual-time tests in this track's labs, from the backoff in lesson 5 to the bank calls in lesson 7, are built from these pieces.

try.title: Break four StepVerifier rules
steps: StepVerifierDemo runs five small tests: one without verify(), a one-day delay under virtual time, expectNoEvent as the first step, a delay built outside the virtual-time supplier, and a TestPublisher driven by hand. (It runs from src/demo, so the lab's build adds reactor-test to the demo classpath.)
Predict which ones pass, which fail, and with what message.
Run it. In part 1, add .verify() to the end of the line and run again.

code.title: StepVerifierDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.test.StepVerifier; import reactor.test.publisher.TestPublisher; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Five StepVerifier habits, most of them shown by breaking them. */ public class StepVerifierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicInteger subscriptions = new AtomicInteger(); Mono<String> charge = Mono.fromCallable(() -> "charged").doOnSubscribe(s -> subscriptions.incrementAndGet()); StepVerifier.create(charge).expectNext("refunded").expectComplete(); // no verify(): nothing runs System.out.println("1. no verify(): subscriptions=" + subscriptions.get() + ", wrong expectation unnoticed"); Duration real = StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("expired")) .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("expired") .verifyComplete(); System.out.println("2. virtual time: one day took " + real.toMillis() + " ms of real time"); try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1))) .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) // subscription counts as an event .expectNext(0L) .verifyComplete(); } catch (AssertionError e) { System.out.println("3. expectNoEvent first: " + e.getMessage()); } Mono<String> builtTooEarly = Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("expired"); // grabs the real clock try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> builtTooEarly) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("expired") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); } catch (AssertionError e) { System.out.println("4. built outside the supplier: " + e.getMessage()); } TestPublisher<String> rates = TestPublisher.create(); StepVerifier.create(rates.flux().map(r -> "EUR/USD " + r)) .then(() -> rates.next("1.08", "1.09")) // push values by hand .expectNext("EUR/USD 1.08", "EUR/USD 1.09") .then(rates::complete) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); System.out.println("5. TestPublisher: passed; the map requested " + (rates.wasRequested() ? "some" : "no") + " items"); } }

alt.title: StepVerifierDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.test.StepVerifier import reactor.test.publisher.TestPublisher import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** Five StepVerifier habits, most of them shown by breaking them. */ fun main() { val subscriptions = AtomicInteger() val charge = Mono.fromCallable { "charged" }.doOnSubscribe { subscriptions.incrementAndGet() } StepVerifier.create(charge).expectNext("refunded").expectComplete() // no verify(): nothing runs println("1. no verify(): subscriptions=${subscriptions.get()}, wrong expectation unnoticed") val real = StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("expired") } .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("expired") .verifyComplete() println("2. virtual time: one day took ${real.toMillis()} ms of real time") try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)) } .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) // subscription counts as an event .expectNext(0L) .verifyComplete() } catch (e: AssertionError) { println("3. expectNoEvent first: ${e.message}") } val builtTooEarly = Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("expired") // grabs the real clock try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { builtTooEarly } .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("expired") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) } catch (e: AssertionError) { println("4. built outside the supplier: ${e.message}") } val rates = TestPublisher.create<String>() StepVerifier.create(rates.flux().map { r -> "EUR/USD $r" }) .then { rates.next("1.08", "1.09") } // push values by hand .expectNext("EUR/USD 1.08", "EUR/USD 1.09") .then { rates.complete() } .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) println("5. TestPublisher: passed; the map requested ${if (rates.wasRequested()) "some" else "no"} items") }

try.expect: Part 1 reports subscriptions=0: without verify() nothing ran, and the wrong expectation (refunded) went unnoticed. After you add .verify(), it throws an AssertionError saying it expected refunded and got charged. Part 2 verifies a full day in a few dozen milliseconds. Part 3 fails with expected no event: onSubscribe(...). Part 4 fails with VerifySubscriber timed out, because the delay holds the real clock. Part 5 passes.

sections.h: Debugging: name the place with checkpoint, watch the signals with log
sections.html:
A stack trace from a reactive chain shows where the error was raised and how the subscription got there. It almost never shows where you wrote the operator that failed. In the demo, Flux.just(120, 80).single() inside a feeRow() method fails with IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item. The top frame is Reactor's MonoSingle, and no frame of the trace is in feeRow(). Lesson 2 of this track explains why: feeRow() only assembled the chain and returned. By the time single() sees the second row, the data pass is running, and the frame of feeRow() is long gone.

checkpoint("fee-row") marks a point in the chain. When an error passes through it, Reactor attaches a suppressed exception that reads Error has been observed at the following site(s): followed by *__checkpoint and fee-row. It is cheap, so put one at the edges of your own pipelines, named after what they do. checkpoint("fee-row", true) also records a stack trace when the chain is assembled, which points at the line in your code, at the cost of capturing that trace every time the chain is built.

Hooks.onOperatorDebug() does that for every operator in the application. The reference guide calls it a last resort because of the cost. For production there is the reactor-tools agent (ReactorDebugAgent.init() as the first line of main), which adds the same information by instrumenting your classes when they load. It is a separate dependency and not in the labs.

Java
Mono<Integer> fee = feeRow(merchant).checkpoint("fee-row");   // name the place, cheaply
Flux<Integer> rows = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2);    // print every signal at this point
Kotlin
val fee: Mono<Int> = feeRow(merchant).checkpoint("fee-row")   // name the place, cheaply
val rows: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2)    // print every signal at this point

log("rows") prints every signal that passes that point: onSubscribe, request(2), onNext(1), onNext(2), cancel(). It is the quickest way to see this track's ideas in a real chain: the demand from lesson 7, the cancellation that take sends upstream, the thread each signal arrives on. It logs through SLF4J when that is on the classpath.

try.title: Find the operator that failed
steps: DebugDemo runs a chain whose single() sees two fee rows, three times: plain, with checkpoint("fee-row"), and with checkpoint("fee-row", true). Then it puts log("rows") between a range and take(2).
Run it. For each of the first three, find the information that tells you where the failing operator was written.
Predict the log output first: which request and which last signal will it show?

code.title: DebugDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.Arrays; /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ public class DebugDemo { // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the merchant has two fee rows, the code expects one static Mono<Integer> feeRow(String merchant) { return Flux.just(120, 80).single(); } static void show(String title, Mono<Integer> chain) { try { chain.block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { boolean mentionsFeeRow = Arrays.stream(e.getStackTrace()).anyMatch(f -> f.getMethodName().equals("feeRow")); System.out.println(title); System.out.println(" " + e); System.out.println(" top frame: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]); System.out.println(" any frame in feeRow(), where single() was written? " + mentionsFeeRow); for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) { s.getMessage().lines() .filter(l -> !l.isBlank() && !l.contains("#block")) .limit(4) .map(l -> l.replace("⇢", "->")) // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach(l -> System.out.println(" " + l.strip())); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { show("1. no help", feeRow("m-1").map(fee -> fee + 1)); show("2. checkpoint(\"fee-row\")", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row").map(fee -> fee + 1)); show("3. checkpoint(\"fee-row\", true)", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row", true).map(fee -> fee + 1)); System.out.println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)"); Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast(); } }

alt.title: DebugDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the merchant has two fee rows, the code expects one private fun feeRow(merchant: String): Mono<Int> = Flux.just(120, 80).single() private fun show(title: String, chain: Mono<Int>) { try { chain.block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { val mentionsFeeRow = e.stackTrace.any { it.methodName.startsWith("feeRow") } println(title) println(" $e") println(" top frame: ${e.stackTrace[0]}") println(" any frame in feeRow(), where single() was written? $mentionsFeeRow") for (s in e.suppressed) { s.message.orEmpty().lines() .filter { it.isNotBlank() && "#block" !in it } .take(4) .map { it.replace("⇢", "->") } // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach { println(" ${it.trim()}") } } } } /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ fun main() { show("1. no help", feeRow("m-1").map { fee -> fee + 1 }) show("2. checkpoint(\"fee-row\")", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row").map { fee -> fee + 1 }) show("3. checkpoint(\"fee-row\", true)", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row", true).map { fee -> fee + 1 }) println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)") Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast() }

try.expect: All three report IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item with MonoSingle as the top frame, and no frame in feeRow(). The plain run gives no clue where it came from. The checkpoint run names fee-row. The run with true adds an assembly trace pointing at the main line where the checkpoint was written. The log shows onSubscribe, request(2), onNext(1), onNext(2) and cancel(): take(2) capped the demand and then cancelled the range.

sections.h: When reactive is still worth it
sections.html:
Reactor is not the default answer for new JVM code in 2026, and the Spring team says so itself. The Spring Framework reference still reads: "If you have a Spring MVC application that works fine, there is no need to change. Imperative programming is the easiest way to write, understand, and debug code." It warns about "the steep learning curve", tells you to "start small and measure the benefits", and adds: "We expect that, for a wide range of applications, the shift is unnecessary." Lesson 1 of this track quoted the same docs on speed: reactive doesn't make applications faster; it lets them scale with fewer threads when calls have latency.

Virtual threads (final in JDK 21) took away most of the thread-count argument. Mark Paluch of the Spring team wrote in 2022, while they were still a preview: "The reasons to use asynchronous programming models go away in many cases if we start with the assumption that our code runs on Virtual Threads." The same post keeps a place for reactive: ReactiveX-style APIs "remain a powerful way to compose concurrent logic and a natural way for dealing with streams", and they are "the right approach for concurrent scenarios in which declarative concurrency (such as scatter-gather) matters."

So here is the position I'd take for your services:

  • For request and response over JDBC, JPA or other blocking clients, use virtual threads and plain imperative code. Don't rewrite a working Quarkus REST or Spring MVC service in Reactor.
  • For streams (server-sent events, WebSockets, Kafka pipelines, anything where demand, cancellation and a loss policy matter), Reactor earns its complexity.
  • For many calls composed with timeouts, retries and fan-out, Reactor's operators are hard to beat. Coroutines, or structured concurrency once it is final, are the imperative alternatives.
  • In a stack that is already reactive end to end (WebClient, R2DBC, Reactor Netty), stay reactive and keep the few blocking calls on boundedElastic.
  • In Kotlin, coroutines give sequential-looking code over the same runtime. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges both ways (awaitSingle(), mono { }, Flow.asFlux()), and Spring maps Mono to suspend and Flux to Flow. The coroutines track builds on that.

Quick check: one Quarkus endpoint reads a payment from Oracle over JDBC, calls the issuer once and returns. Another relays an issuer's live event stream to browsers that read at different speeds. Which one needs request(n), and why? (The second. The first waits for one reply, which a virtual thread does cheaply. The second has a fast producer and slow consumers, and only demand or a loss policy stops events piling up in memory for the slow ones.)

refs.title: Embracing Virtual Threads (Spring blog, Mark Paluch, 2022)
Spring Framework reference: Spring WebFlux overview, applicability and performance

analogy: Cold is video on demand: everyone who presses play gets the film from the start, and the studio streams one copy per viewer. share() is live TV: one broadcast, and if you switch on late, you missed the start. replay(1) is live TV that shows you the last scene when you switch on. cache() is a recorder that keeps the whole broadcast forever, so every newcomer can watch from the beginning, and the recordings pile up. A sink is the studio's microphone, which only one presenter may speak into at a time. The analogy breaks at the end of the evening: a TV station keeps broadcasting to an empty room, while refCount switches the transmitter off when the last viewer leaves.
world: Picture a payment operations service. A Kafka consumer pushes authorization events into a sink, and dashboards follow them over server-sent events: that is a multicast directBestEffort sink with a thread-safe emit, because Kafka listener threads run concurrently and dashboards come and go. The FX rates come from one provider connection that a dozen screens share with replay(1).refCount(1, grace). The fee schedule is read from Oracle at most once every five minutes with Mono.cache(ttl). Every one of those has timing in it, so each gets a virtual-time test that runs in milliseconds in CI. And when a new service is plain request and response over Oracle, you build it on virtual threads instead.
mistake: The most common mistake is calling tryEmitNext on a sink from several threads and ignoring the result. It looks safe because the sink is "thread-safe", and it is, in the sense that it detects the concurrent call and refuses it with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED instead of corrupting itself. The refused item is simply gone. In tests with one thread, everything arrives; in production, with four Kafka listener threads, events go missing with no log line. Use emitNext(item, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))), or serialize the calls yourself, and write a test that emits from several threads at once.

compare.title: A hot event hub and a shared feed in Reactor and Kotlin

java.title: PaymentEvents.java (Reactor)
java.html: // Reactor: a hub that listener threads push into, and a shared rate feed private final Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> events = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); void publish(PaymentEvent e) { events.emitNext(e, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); } Flux<PaymentEvent> live() { return events.asFlux(); } Flux<Rate> rates = provider.rates() .replay(1) // late subscribers get the latest rate .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); // disconnect 5 s after the last one leaves

kotlin.title: PaymentEvents.kt (coroutines)
kotlin.html: // Kotlin coroutines: SharedFlow for events, StateFlow for "the latest value" private val events = MutableSharedFlow<PaymentEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1_000) fun publish(e: PaymentEvent) { check(events.tryEmit(e)) { "subscribers are too slow" } // thread-safe; suspend emit() waits instead } val live: SharedFlow<PaymentEvent> = events.asSharedFlow() val rates: StateFlow<Rate?> = provider.rates() .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null) // latest rate, stop 5 s after the last leaves

compare.note: The shapes match: a multicast sink is close to a MutableSharedFlow, and replay(1).refCount(1, grace) is close to stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null). The differences are in concurrency and lifetime. A MutableSharedFlow accepts emissions from any number of threads at once; its tryEmit fails only when the buffer is full, and emit suspends instead. A Reactor sink refuses concurrent emissions unless you retry or serialize. And stateIn and shareIn need a CoroutineScope: the shared upstream lives in that scope and is cancelled with it, which is structured concurrency. Reactor's sharing lives as long as subscribers keep it alive. StateFlow also always has a current value and skips values equal to the last one, which replay(1) does not. The coroutines track covers SharedFlow and StateFlow in detail.

worked.title: Test a payment-status poller in milliseconds

steps.say: After a payment is sent to the bank, a poller asks for its status every 30 seconds until it is final, and gives up after 5 minutes. A real-time test would take 90 seconds for the happy path and 5 minutes for the timeout. Here is the code under test.
steps.code: Mono<Status> awaitFinal(String paymentId) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // poll every 30 s .concatMap(tick -> api.status(paymentId)) // one call at a time .filter(Status::isFinal) .next() // first final status, then stop polling .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5)); }

alt.html: fun awaitFinal(paymentId: String): Mono<Status> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // poll every 30 s .concatMap { api.status(paymentId) } // one call at a time .filter(Status::isFinal) .next() // first final status, then stop polling .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5))

steps.say: The happy path: the fake API answers PENDING twice, then SETTLED. Under virtual time the polls happen at 30, 60 and 90 seconds of fake time. expectNoEvent(90 s) proves nothing came out earlier, and the settled status arrives exactly at 90 s.
steps.code: FakeStatusApi api = new FakeStatusApi(PENDING, PENDING, SETTLED); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new StatusPoller(api).awaitFinal("p-1")) // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third poll .expectNext(SETTLED) .verifyComplete(); assertThat(api.calls()).isEqualTo(3);

alt.html: val api = FakeStatusApi(PENDING, PENDING, SETTLED) StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { StatusPoller(api).awaitFinal("p-1") } // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third poll .expectNext(SETTLED) .verifyComplete() assertThat(api.calls()).isEqualTo(3)

steps.say: The timeout path: the payment never settles. Jump the clock to the deadline and expect the TimeoutException. Keep a real-time limit on verify as well, so a mistake makes the test fail in one second instead of hanging.
steps.code: FakeStatusApi stuck = new FakeStatusApi(PENDING); // pending forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new StatusPoller(stuck).awaitFinal("p-2")) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException.class) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // 5. a real-time safety net

alt.html: val stuck = FakeStatusApi(PENDING) // pending forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { StatusPoller(stuck).awaitFinal("p-2") } .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException::class.java) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 5. a real-time safety net

steps.say: Both tests run in a few milliseconds. If one of them hangs instead, look at where the poller is built: Flux.interval and timeout pick their scheduler when the chain is assembled, so a poller created before withVirtualTime runs on the real clock. The same goes for a Mono built once in a @BeforeEach and kept in a field.

lab.title: A payment-event hub and two shared feeds
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail.

PaymentEventHub: choose the sink from the Javadoc of live() (only events after you subscribed, nothing kept while nobody listens, survives every subscriber leaving). Then make publish safe for 8 threads at once, and return a read-only view from live().
RateFeeds.shareWithLatest: one upstream connection, the latest rate for late subscribers, and a disconnect when the last subscriber leaves.
RateFeeds.cacheFor: load at most once per ttl. Read how the test controls the clock with VirtualTimeScheduler.getOrSet() and advanceTimeBy.
Run the tests until all six pass, then once more: the 8-thread test must pass every time.
hints: If the hot test finds event 0 in the early subscriber's list, your sink kept events published before anyone subscribed: multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() does that. The same sink fails the "every subscriber has left" test with a completion.

If the 8-thread test receives fewer than 16,000 events, you ignored the result of tryEmitNext. If it reports crashed threads, you used EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST, which throws on FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED.
share() fails the late-subscriber test (no latest value); cache() and replay(1).autoConnect() fail the disconnect test (they never cancel upstream).
Mono.cache() with no argument never reloads. There is an overload that takes a Duration.
lab.done: All six tests in HotPublishersTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: A one-hour test that runs in milliseconds
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a StepVerifier test for Mono.delay(Duration.ofHours(1)).thenReturn("expired") that proves nothing is emitted before the hour is up, then expired and completion, runs in milliseconds, and can't hang the build. Then compare.

answer.html: StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofHours(1)).thenReturn("expired")) .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofHours(1)) .expectNext("expired") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1));

alt.html: StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { Mono.delay(Duration.ofHours(1)).thenReturn("expired") } .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofHours(1)) .expectNext("expired") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1))

recap: share() (publish().refCount()) gives late subscribers only new items; replay(n).refCount() replays the last n; cache() replays everything forever. refCount disconnects when the last subscriber leaves, autoConnect never does.
Sinks push values from ordinary code. tryEmitNext refuses concurrent calls with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED: check the result, or use emitNext with busyLooping.
A multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() sink shuts down when its last subscriber leaves; directBestEffort() keeps no buffer and survives an empty room.
StepVerifier runs nothing until verify(). Give it a timeout, build the publisher inside the withVirtualTime supplier, and call expectSubscription() before expectNoEvent.
checkpoint("name") tags errors with a place in your chain cheaply; log() prints every signal at one point.

Reactive earns its complexity for streams, backpressure and composed concurrency. For request and response over blocking libraries, the Spring team itself says imperative code on virtual threads is enough.

explain.prompt: A teammate is building a dashboard backend: a Kafka consumer receives payment events and a dozen browsers should see them live, plus the current FX rate. Explain which Reactor pieces you would use, what can silently go wrong with each, and how you would test it.
explain.answer: For the events I'd use a multicast sink, directBestEffort(), because each browser only needs events from the moment it connects, nothing should pile up while nobody watches, and the hub must keep working after every browser disconnects (the buffered flavour shuts down when its last subscriber leaves). The Kafka listener threads would publish with emitNext and a busyLooping handler, because tryEmitNext refuses concurrent calls and the refused event just disappears. For the FX rate I'd wrap the provider feed in replay(1).refCount(1, grace): one connection, new browsers get the current rate at once, and the connection closes a few seconds after the last browser leaves. share() would leave new browsers blank until the next tick, and cache() would never disconnect and would keep every rate. To test it I'd use TestPublisher for the provider, a multi-threaded test for the hub with a start latch, and StepVerifier.withVirtualTime for anything with time in it, always with verify(Duration) so a bug fails fast instead of hanging.

deeper.html:
Connecting by hand. publish() and replay() return a ConnectableFlux. Besides refCount and autoConnect, you can call connect() yourself once every subscriber is in place, and dispose the returned Disposable to disconnect. That suits a startup sequence that wires several consumers before any data should flow.

Context instead of ThreadLocal. Because a chain hops threads, a ThreadLocal such as an MDC trace id doesn't follow it. Reactor's Context does: write it at the bottom with contextWrite(Context.of("traceId", id)) and read it upstream with Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> ...). It travels from the subscriber toward the source, so a contextWrite above the reader is invisible to it. With the Micrometer context-propagation library on the classpath, Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() (Reactor 3.5.3+) restores ThreadLocals such as the MDC around each operator; it isn't in the labs.

BlockHound in tests. Calling BlockHound.install() at the start of a test run makes any blocking call on a non-blocking thread throw BlockingOperationError, which catches the JDBC call on an event loop from the schedulers lesson before production does. On JDK 13+ it needs -XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods.

Backpressure in tests. StepVerifier.create(flux, 0) starts with no demand, and thenRequest(n) adds it step by step. That is how the lab of lesson 7 of this track checked which tick a slow subscriber receives.
